evals.prompt:
Can you synthesize these user interviews? We did 8 interviews with mid-market operations managers at companies using our workflow automation tool. Research question: Why do users abandon setup after the initial login? We're in problem discovery — we don't have a solution yet. Here are my raw notes:

---
P1 - Ops Manager, 200-person logistics company
- said they were excited when first signed up
- got into the product, couldn't figure out where to start
- 'there's too many options, I didn't know which one was for me'
- they tried the template library, none of the templates matched their industry
- gave up after about 20 min
- uses Zapier currently but it's 'duct tape'
- their team does a lot of exception handling — standard flows don't work for them
- would pay for something that handles edge cases better

P2 - Ops Manager, healthcare staffing firm
- came in through a LinkedIn ad
- set up an account, saw the dashboard, felt overwhelmed
- tried to build a workflow from scratch, got stuck on the trigger configuration
- 'I kept hitting error messages and didn't know what they meant'
- gave up, came back a week later, forgot where they left off — no indication of progress
- biggest pain: no onboarding guide specific to their role or industry
- mentioned their team has 3 people who would use it if it was simpler
- currently using spreadsheets + email chains

P3 - RevOps Lead, SaaS startup (~80 employees)
- more technical than others, got further in setup
- completed 2 workflows but they broke after a few days
- couldn't tell what broke or why — no error logging visible to them
- had to contact support, took 3 days to get a response
- 'I just gave up. I can't run my ops on something this fragile'
- uses Make.com now
- would switch back if reliability was better

P4 - Office Manager, professional services
- not technical, panicked when she saw the interface
- tried templates, found one that was close but couldn't customize it
- 'I'm not a developer. I don't know what a webhook is'
- wants something that asks her what she wants to do in plain English
- still in trial, hasn't canceled but hasn't set anything up
- biggest concern: what happens if something breaks? Who fixes it?

P5 - Ops Director, e-commerce brand
- completed setup but said it took 'way too long'
- had to watch 4 YouTube videos to figure out the trigger logic
- 'the documentation is either too basic or too advanced, nothing in the middle'
- set up 3 workflows that are working
- main complaint: can't see all workflows in one place, has to click into each one
- wants a dashboard that shows workflow health across everything
- likely to renew, but said they'd recommend it more if onboarding was better

P6 - Operations Manager, construction company
- never made it past the first screen
- signed up because their company mandated a 'digital transformation' initiative
- not personally motivated to figure it out
- 'nobody trained me on this, I don't have time to learn a new tool'
- suggested the product needed a 'this is what you do first' guide
- would engage if their manager told them to — pure compliance user

P7 - Ops Manager, fintech startup
- had a specific use case in mind (automating invoice approvals)
- searched for a template, found one, tried to customize it for their approval chain
- got stuck because the tool didn't support conditional branching with more than 2 levels
- 'my process isn't that complex, but apparently it's too complex for this'
- ended up building a workaround that felt fragile
- told me they'd 'live with it for now' but wouldn't build more on top of it
- asked if conditional logic improvements were on the roadmap

P8 - Head of Ops, digital agency
- very positive overall, completed setup, has 8 active workflows
- said the key was finding a template that was 80% right
- spent significant time customizing but was OK with it
- main feedback: the template search is broken — 'I found my template by accident'
- mentioned their team trained themselves, 'the product is learnable but not teachable'
- would recommend to others in their network
- suggested the product needed better discoverability, not necessarily simpler features
---
evals.expected_output: Structured synthesis with: overview, 3–6 key themes with frequency counts and quotes, pain points ordered by severity, behavioral observations vs. stated preferences, opportunity areas framed as user needs, signal quality assessment, and offer for follow-on artifacts.
expectations: Overview accurately summarizes the research context (8 participants, ops managers, workflow automation, problem discovery)
Key themes include setup/onboarding friction and are grounded in specific participant observations with frequency counts
At least one theme captures the tension between technical and non-technical users
Pain points are ordered by frequency/severity signal and each cites specific participants
Behavioral observations section notes where stated preferences diverge from observed behavior (e.g., P8 succeeded despite the same problems others cited)
Opportunity areas are framed as user needs, not features
P3's reliability concern is treated as a distinct pain point from the onboarding friction
P6's compliance-driven usage is noted as a segment-specific finding
Signal quality section is honest about what's strong vs. directional
Offer for follow-on artifacts is made at the end

evals.prompt:
Synthesize these interviews. Context: we're validating a solution concept — a 'campaign planning hub' that sits upstream of campaign creation in our marketing platform. We interviewed 10 people: 6 enterprise marketing managers and 4 SMB marketing owners. Research question: Does the concept resonate? What's missing or wrong about it?

Please include a JTBD framing at the end.

---
P1 - Enterprise marketing manager, SaaS company (5000 employees)
- Immediately understood the concept, said 'this is what's missing'
- Their current process: kickoff doc in Google Docs, strategy in a separate deck, assets created without context from either
- 'By the time something gets made, nobody remembers why we're making it'
- Worried about adoption — 'another tool my team has to log into'
- Wants it embedded in existing workflow, not a new step
- Would use it personally but not sure their team would

P2 - SMB marketing owner, e-commerce, solo marketer
- Confused by the concept at first — 'what's the difference between planning and just doing?'
- Once explained, said 'oh, I do this in my head, I'd never write it down'
- Not a problem for her — she's the only one who needs to know the context
- More interested in execution tools than planning tools
- Wouldn't pay separately for this — 'it should just be part of the campaign builder'

P3 - Enterprise marketing manager, financial services
- Strong pain around approvals — campaigns go back and forth because reviewers don't have context
- 'I spend 30% of my time just explaining background to people who need to approve things'
- The planning hub concept resonated specifically for its role in reducing approval friction
- Wants a way to attach the plan to the campaign so approvers see it automatically
- Less interested in the AI generation aspects — wants a structured form, not freeform

P4 - SMB marketing owner, professional services, 3-person team
- Understood the concept, said 'we're bad at this'
- Their team creates campaigns reactively, no planning upstream
- Would use it if it was fast — 'I don't have time to fill out a long brief'
- Wanted AI to pre-fill as much as possible based on past campaigns
- Pain: every campaign feels like starting from zero

P5 - Enterprise marketing manager, B2B tech
- Most sophisticated interviewee — runs a 12-person marketing team
- Already has a planning process (Asana + a custom brief template)
- Skeptical: 'I don't need another place to do this'
- But interested in the activation piece — turning the plan into campaign inputs automatically
- 'If it could generate the first draft from my brief, I'd use it'
- Doesn't want to give up their existing planning tools

P6 - Enterprise marketing manager, healthcare
- Very interested — 'campaign context is constantly lost in our org'
- Team of 8 marketers, lots of handoffs between strategy and execution
- Current process: brief in email, assets created by agency without seeing the brief
- Concept resonated strongly for handoff use case
- Concerned about confidentiality — 'we have campaigns that can't be shared broadly'

P7 - SMB marketing owner, retail, 2 people
- Confused by 'upstream planning' framing
- Once shown mockup, engaged more positively
- Main interest: 'I want to remember why I made decisions six months ago'
- Thinks of it as institutional memory more than planning
- Would use a lightweight version, not a full structured brief

P8 - Enterprise marketing manager, edtech
- Runs campaign sprints, wants a 'sprint brief' concept
- Planning hub concept aligned with how they already think
- Wants integration with Jira and Notion — their team lives there
- Won't use something that creates more export/import steps
- Highlighted: the value is not in creating the brief, it's in the brief being *visible* throughout execution

P9 - SMB marketing owner, B2B SaaS startup
- Eager to try — 'I've been looking for something like this'
- Their pain: campaigns launch without a clear goal, then they can't evaluate performance
- Wants success criteria embedded in the plan and carried forward into reporting
- AI pre-fill was the most exciting feature mentioned
- Would replace their current Google Doc brief template with this

P10 - Enterprise marketing manager, consumer goods
- Mixed reaction — planning isn't their bottleneck
- 'We plan too much and execute too little'
- Worried the hub would add process overhead
- But interested in the AI-driven insight angle — 'if it could tell me what's worked before, that's useful'
- Would use it if it was lightweight and fast, not if it was another structured form
---
evals.expected_output: Structured synthesis that clearly distinguishes enterprise and SMB user perspectives, identifies where the concept resonated vs. fell flat, and surfaces the core tension (structured planning vs. execution speed). JTBD framing at the end. Signal quality section honest about the mixed results.
expectations: Overview accurately describes the mixed participant pool (6 enterprise, 4 SMB) and solution validation context
Key themes clearly distinguish enterprise vs. SMB perspectives — they are not flattened into a single view
The core tension between 'planning as valuable' (enterprise) and 'planning as overhead' (SMB) is surfaced as a finding, not smoothed over
Behavioral observations notes that P5 (already has a process) and P10 (plans too much) represent an important counter-signal
P8's insight about visibility throughout execution is called out — it's one of the sharpest observations in the set
Opportunity areas are framed as user needs, not product features
Signal quality section is honest that concept resonance was split and the SMB case is weaker
JTBD section includes 3 distinct jobs across the enterprise and SMB segments
Offer for follow-on artifacts is made

evals.prompt:
I have notes from 6 interviews but they're really rough — some are just a few bullet points. Research question: How do engineering managers currently handle 1:1s and performance feedback? We're evaluating whether to build a 1:1 management tool. Stage: early problem discovery. Please synthesize and also give me an OST branch structure.

---
P1 - EM at Series B startup
- does 1:1s weekly, no structure
- keeps notes in Apple Notes, can't find them later
- feels like 1:1s 'could be more useful'
- direct reports sometimes don't come prepared

P2 - EM at enterprise (3000 employees)
- uses a shared Google Doc with each report
- works ok but doesn't scale — has 9 direct reports now
- performance review season is chaos
- 'I'm writing the same things multiple times in different systems'
- HR system doesn't talk to where he keeps his notes

P3 - EM at mid-size tech co
- very short notes — said she tracks action items in Jira
- doesn't keep running notes on people
- 'I just remember'
- worried about saying the wrong thing if notes are written down (legal)
- thinks a tool would make 1:1s feel transactional

P4 - EM at Series C startup
- uses Notion, has a template
- pretty happy with current setup
- main pain: hard to see patterns across time
- 'I know things have improved but I can't show the evidence'
- wants to demonstrate growth of their reports to leadership
- 'I'm advocating for people without the receipts'

P5 - EM at large enterprise
- uses the company's HR system for everything
- hates it — 'designed for HR not for managers'
- fills it out because required, doesn't find it useful
- keeps a 'real' doc separately
- performance reviews take 2 full days, most of it is reformatting and copying

P6 - EM at early-stage startup (seed)
- team of 3, informal 1:1s
- 'we just talk, I don't need a tool'
- but mentioned they're growing fast, 'I know this won't scale'
- interested in what a lightweight tool would look like
- doesn't want their 1:1s to feel like a performance review
---
evals.expected_output: Synthesis that's honest about the thin signal quality (rough notes, only 6 participants). Identifies the key themes and pain points, notes P3's important counter-signal (skepticism about written notes), and provides an OST branch structure. Should not overstate confidence given the data quality.
expectations: Overview is honest that the notes are rough and the sample is small (6 participants)
Signal quality section explicitly notes limitations — thin notes, small sample, only 6 participants — and says what requires more signal before acting on it
P3's skepticism (legal concerns, transactional feel) is treated as a meaningful counter-signal, not dismissed
P4's insight about 'advocating without receipts' is called out — it's the sharpest articulation of the pain
Behavioral observations notes the gap between P3 ('I just remember') and P5 (keeps a shadow doc outside the official system)
Opportunity areas do not overstate confidence given the thin notes
OST section maps findings to opportunity branches without adding solutions
Offer for follow-on artifacts is made
